title: Data Structures and Algorithms for placements

skills.name: Big-O and complexity analysis
skills.notes: Big-O describes how the running time or memory of an algorithm grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. We usually reason about the worst case unless told otherwise. Count how many times the dominant operation runs: a single loop over n items is O(n), two nested loops over n are O(n^2), and a loop that halves the problem each step is O(log n). Sequential blocks add, nested blocks multiply, and we keep only the largest term, so n^2 + n becomes O(n^2). Space complexity counts extra memory beyond the input, including the recursion stack. Be able to rank common classes: 1, log n, n, n log n, n^2, 2^n, n!. In interviews, always state both time and space and justify them aloud.

skills.name: Arrays and indexing

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview arrays and strings

skills.notes: An array stores elements in contiguous memory, which gives O(1) random access by index and excellent cache behaviour. Inserting or deleting in the middle costs O(n) because later elements must shift; appending to a dynamic array is amortised O(1) because capacity doubles occasionally. Indices run from 0 to n-1, and off-by-one mistakes at the boundaries are the most common bug, so check the first and last element and the empty array. Learn to traverse, reverse in place, rotate, find max and min, and remove duplicates from a sorted array. In-place algorithms use O(1) extra space by swapping or overwriting. Know the difference between array length and the last valid index. Many interview problems reduce to a clean single pass over an array, so practise tracking a running value like a maximum or a count.

skills.name: Strings and character handling

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview arrays and strings

skills.notes: A string is a sequence of characters, and in many languages such as Java and Python it is immutable, so building a result with repeated concatenation inside a loop costs O(n^2); use a StringBuilder or a list and join instead. Know how to iterate characters, compare strings lexicographically, reverse, check palindromes, count character frequency with an array of 26 or a map, and test anagrams by comparing counts or sorted forms. Substring extraction costs O(length) in most languages. ASCII uses 128 values while Unicode needs more, so state your alphabet assumptions. Watch for case sensitivity, spaces and empty strings. Comparing two strings with equals checks content, while the double equals operator in some languages compares references, a classic source of bugs.

skills.name: Recursion
skills.notes: Recursion solves a problem by calling the same function on smaller inputs until a base case stops it. Every recursive function needs a base case that returns directly and a recursive step that moves strictly toward it; missing either causes infinite recursion and a stack overflow. Each call uses a stack frame, so depth d costs O(d) space. Trace small inputs by hand to see the call tree. Time complexity follows a recurrence: factorial is T(n)=T(n-1)+O(1)=O(n), while naive Fibonacci is T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2), which is exponential because subproblems repeat. Recursion pairs naturally with trees, divide and conquer and backtracking. Any recursion can be rewritten with an explicit stack. Learn to define what the function returns, trust it on smaller inputs, and combine results.

skills.name: Elementary sorting
skills.notes: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs, selection sort picks the minimum of the unsorted part and places it at the front, and insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by inserting each next element into place. All three run in O(n^2) worst case with O(1) extra space. Insertion sort is O(n) on nearly sorted input and is used inside real library sorts for small arrays. Selection sort always does about n^2/2 comparisons but only n swaps. Stability means equal elements keep their original relative order; insertion and bubble sort are stable while the usual selection sort is not. Be able to write insertion sort from memory, explain loop invariants, and state why comparison sorts cannot beat O(n log n) in general.

skills.name: Binary search

resources.title: Binary Search on LeetCode explore card

skills.notes: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array by comparing with the middle element and discarding half the range, giving O(log n) time and O(1) space iteratively. The array must be sorted, otherwise the logic is invalid. Keep invariants clear: with low and high inclusive, loop while low <= high, compute mid = low + (high - low) / 2 to avoid integer overflow, and set low = mid + 1 or high = mid - 1. Off-by-one errors and infinite loops come from updating with mid instead of mid plus or minus one. The same idea works on any monotonic predicate, for example finding the smallest value that satisfies a condition, which powers lower bound, upper bound and search on the answer. Know how to return the insertion index when the target is absent.

skills.name: Hash tables and maps
skills.notes: A hash table maps keys to values by passing the key through a hash function that picks a bucket, giving average O(1) insert, lookup and delete. Collisions happen when different keys land in the same bucket and are handled by chaining, with a list per bucket, or by open addressing, probing for another slot. With a poor hash function or adversarial keys, operations degrade to O(n) in the worst case. The load factor, entries divided by buckets, triggers resizing, which rehashes everything and is amortised O(1) per insert. Keys must be hashable and immutable, and iteration order is not sorted in a plain hash map. Typical uses are counting frequencies, detecting duplicates, two-sum style lookups and grouping by a computed key. A hash set stores only keys and answers membership queries quickly.

skills.name: Two pointers

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview chapter on arrays

skills.notes: The two-pointer technique uses two indices that move through a sequence to avoid a nested loop, often turning O(n^2) into O(n). In the opposite-ends pattern one pointer starts at the left and one at the right, and you move one inward based on a comparison; this solves pair-sum on a sorted array, container with most water and palindrome checks. In the same-direction pattern a slow pointer marks the write position while a fast pointer scans, used to remove duplicates or move zeros in place. The key is a clear rule for which pointer moves and a proof that no valid answer is skipped. Sorting first can enable the technique at a cost of O(n log n). Always handle empty and single-element inputs, and be careful that pointers do not cross when they should not.

skills.name: Sliding window
skills.notes: A sliding window maintains a contiguous subarray or substring defined by left and right boundaries, expanding the right edge and shrinking the left edge while tracking a running sum, count or set. For a fixed-size window of length k you add the new element and remove the one that leaves, giving O(n) rather than O(nk). For a variable-size window you expand until a condition breaks, then shrink until it holds again, which handles longest substring without repeating characters and smallest subarray with sum at least a target. Each pointer only moves forward, so total work is O(n) even though there is a loop inside a loop. Use a hash map or array of counts to track window contents. Decide clearly whether the window is valid after each expansion, and update the best answer at the right moment.

skills.name: Prefix sums
skills.notes: A prefix sum array stores in prefix[i] the sum of the first i elements, so the sum of any range from l to r (inclusive) is prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing. This turns repeated range-sum queries from O(n) each into O(1) each. Use an extra leading zero so empty ranges and ranges starting at index 0 need no special case. The idea extends to 2D grids with a rectangle formula, to counting subarrays with a given sum using a hash map of earlier prefix values, and to difference arrays that apply many range updates and recover the final array with one prefix pass. Beware of integer overflow with large sums and off-by-one errors in the indices. Prefix sums only work well when the array is static or updates are rare.

skills.name: Linked lists

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview linked lists

skills.notes: A singly linked list stores each element in a node with a value and a pointer to the next node; there is no random access, so reaching the kth node costs O(k). Insertion or deletion is O(1) once you hold the previous node, but finding it costs O(n). Always handle the empty list and the head separately, or use a dummy node before the head to simplify edge cases. Core techniques are reversing a list by rewiring pointers, detecting a cycle with slow and fast pointers, finding the middle with the same trick, merging two sorted lists, and removing the nth node from the end with a gap of n between two pointers. Draw boxes and arrows before coding, and save the next pointer before overwriting it. Doubly linked lists add a previous pointer for O(1) removal given a node.

skills.name: Stacks

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview stacks and queues

skills.notes: A stack is a last-in first-out structure with push, pop and peek, all O(1) when built on an array or linked list. Popping from an empty stack is an error you must guard against. Stacks model nested or reversed behaviour: the function call stack, undo history, backtracking and expression evaluation. Classic problems include balanced parentheses, where each closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opening one, evaluating postfix expressions, converting infix to postfix, and implementing a queue with two stacks. Any recursion can be rewritten iteratively with an explicit stack, which avoids stack overflow on deep inputs. When a problem mentions the most recent item, matching pairs or reversing order, think stack first. Always check emptiness before peeking, and remember the stack must be empty at the end for balanced input.

skills.name: Queues and deques

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview stacks and queues

skills.notes: A queue is first-in first-out: enqueue adds at the back and dequeue removes from the front, both O(1) with a linked list or a circular array. Using a plain array and removing from index 0 costs O(n), which is a common mistake. A deque, or double-ended queue, allows O(1) insertion and removal at both ends and powers sliding window maximum and 0-1 breadth-first search. A priority queue is different: it removes the highest-priority element, not the oldest. Queues model waiting lines, task scheduling, buffering and level-order traversal in breadth-first search. A circular buffer reuses space by wrapping indices with a modulus, and you must distinguish full from empty, typically by tracking size or leaving one slot unused. Know how to implement a stack with two queues and a queue with two stacks.

skills.name: Monotonic stack
skills.notes: A monotonic stack keeps its elements in sorted order, increasing or decreasing from bottom to top, by popping elements that would break the order before pushing a new one. It answers next greater element, previous smaller element, daily temperatures, largest rectangle in a histogram and stock span questions in O(n) total, because each element is pushed once and popped at most once. Store indices rather than values when you need distances or positions. When a new element arrives, every popped element has just found its answer: the new element is its next greater or smaller value. After the loop, elements left on the stack have no answer, often meaning a default such as minus one. Decide the direction of monotonicity from the question, for example a decreasing stack for next greater element.

skills.name: Merge sort and quicksort
skills.notes: Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively and merges the two sorted halves in linear time, giving O(n log n) in every case with O(n) extra space and a stable result. Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the array so smaller values are left and larger values are right, and recurses on both sides; it is O(n log n) on average with O(log n) stack space but O(n^2) in the worst case, for example an already sorted array with the first element as pivot. Random or median-of-three pivots make the worst case unlikely. Quicksort is usually faster in practice because of cache behaviour, while merge sort suits linked lists and external sorting. Know that comparison sorting needs Omega(n log n) comparisons, and that counting sort breaks this for small integer ranges.

skills.name: Heaps and priority queues
skills.notes: A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent is smaller than or equal to its children in a min-heap, or larger in a max-heap. For index i the children are at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and the parent at (i-1)/2. Insert appends at the end and sifts up in O(log n); removing the root swaps it with the last element and sifts down in O(log n); reading the root is O(1). Building a heap from n elements with bottom-up heapify costs O(n), not O(n log n). Heaps implement priority queues and power top-k problems, merging k sorted lists, running medians with two heaps and Dijkstra. To keep the k largest values use a min-heap of size k so the smallest of them sits on top. A heap does not keep all elements sorted, only the root is guaranteed extreme.

skills.name: Bit manipulation

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview bit manipulation chapter

skills.notes: Bit manipulation works directly on the binary representation of integers using AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts. A left shift by k multiplies by 2^k and a right shift divides by 2^k, rounding toward negative infinity for signed values. To test bit i use (x >> i) & 1, to set it use x | (1 << i), to clear it use x & ~(1 << i) and to toggle it use x ^ (1 << i). XOR of a number with itself is zero and with zero is itself, which finds the single non-duplicated number in an array. The expression x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so repeating it counts set bits, and x & (x - 1) == 0 tests for a power of two when x is positive. Know that negative numbers use two's complement, and that bit masks can represent subsets of up to about 30 items.

skills.name: Number theory basics

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview math chapter

skills.notes: Interview number theory focuses on gcd, primes, modular arithmetic and simple counting. The Euclidean algorithm computes gcd(a, b) by repeating gcd(b, a mod b) until the remainder is zero, in O(log min(a, b)) steps, and lcm(a, b) equals a times b divided by gcd, ideally computed as a / gcd * b to avoid overflow. To test whether n is prime you only need to check divisors up to the square root of n, giving O(sqrt n); the Sieve of Eratosthenes lists all primes up to n in about O(n log log n). Modular arithmetic lets you keep numbers small: (a + b) mod m, (a * b) mod m and fast exponentiation by squaring in O(log n). Division under a modulus needs the modular inverse, so never just divide. Remember that 1 is not prime and 2 is the only even prime.

skills.name: Backtracking

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview recursion chapter

skills.notes: Backtracking builds candidates step by step and abandons a path as soon as it cannot lead to a valid solution, undoing the last choice to try another. The template is: choose an option, recurse, then unchoose. It explores a decision tree depth first, so subsets of n items have 2^n leaves and permutations n! leaves; pruning invalid branches early is what makes it practical. Typical problems are generating subsets, permutations and combinations, N-Queens, sudoku and word search. Keep a current path and a result list, and copy the path when you add it to the results, otherwise later changes corrupt stored answers. Avoid duplicates by sorting and skipping equal neighbours at the same level. State the time complexity honestly as exponential, then explain the pruning that reduces it in practice.

skills.name: Binary trees and traversals

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview trees and graphs

skills.notes: A binary tree node has at most two children, left and right. The height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path, a leaf has no children, and a tree of n nodes has n minus one edges. Depth-first traversals visit nodes recursively: preorder is root, left, right; inorder is left, root, right; postorder is left, right, root. Breadth-first or level-order traversal uses a queue and visits nodes level by level. All traversals take O(n) time; recursive ones use O(h) stack space where h is the height, which is O(n) for a skewed tree and O(log n) for a balanced one. Most tree problems are solved by defining what to compute for a node from its children's answers. Handle the null node as the base case. Be able to write all four traversals both recursively and iteratively.

skills.name: Binary search trees

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview BST chapter

skills.notes: In a binary search tree, every node's left subtree holds values smaller than the node and its right subtree holds larger values, applied recursively to the whole subtree, not just to the immediate children. This makes search, insert and delete O(h) where h is the height: O(log n) when balanced but O(n) for a degenerate tree built from sorted input. An inorder traversal of a valid BST gives the values in sorted order, which is the easiest way to validate one. Validate with min and max bounds passed down the recursion, because checking only each node against its direct children misses violations deeper down. Deleting a node with two children replaces it with its inorder successor, the smallest node in the right subtree. Self-balancing trees such as AVL and red-black trees keep the height at O(log n) with rotations.

skills.name: Tree recursion patterns

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview trees chapter

skills.notes: Many tree problems share one recursive shape: handle the null base case, ask the left and right subtrees for an answer, and combine them with the current node. Height is one plus the maximum of the child heights. Diameter is the longest path between any two nodes and is found by computing height while tracking the best sum of left and right heights at each node, not just at the root. The lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a general tree is the first node where the search finds one target in each subtree; in a BST you can walk down using the values. A tree is balanced if the heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one at every node. Path sum problems pass the remaining target down. Decide whether information flows down as parameters or up as return values, and avoid recomputing heights repeatedly inside the recursion.

skills.name: Tries
skills.notes: A trie, or prefix tree, stores strings character by character along root-to-node paths, with a flag on nodes where a word ends. Insert, search and prefix lookup each take O(L) time where L is the length of the word, independent of how many words are stored. Each node holds children in an array of 26 or in a hash map, trading memory for speed. Tries excel at autocomplete, prefix counting, dictionary word search and longest common prefix. A hash set can test whole-word membership in average O(L) too, but it cannot answer prefix queries without scanning. The main cost is memory, because many nodes can be created for sparse data. Be careful to distinguish a prefix from a complete word using the end-of-word flag, so searching for app does not succeed merely because apple was inserted.

skills.name: Graph representations
skills.notes: A graph is a set of vertices and edges, which may be directed or undirected and weighted or unweighted. The adjacency list stores for each vertex a list of its neighbours and takes O(V + E) space, which suits sparse graphs and makes iterating neighbours efficient. The adjacency matrix is a V by V grid taking O(V^2) space, but it answers whether an edge exists in O(1), which suits dense graphs. An undirected edge must be stored in both directions. Degree counts edges at a vertex; in a directed graph there are in-degree and out-degree. A graph with V vertices can have at most V(V-1)/2 undirected edges. Many interview inputs are implicit graphs, such as grids where neighbours are up, down, left and right, or words connected by one-letter changes. Decide the representation before writing traversal code.

skills.name: Breadth-first search
skills.notes: Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level from a source using a queue and a visited set. Mark a node visited when you enqueue it, not when you dequeue it, otherwise the same node can be queued many times. On an unweighted graph BFS finds the shortest path in number of edges, because it reaches every node by the fewest edges first. Time is O(V + E) with an adjacency list and space is O(V) for the queue and visited set. For a grid, treat each cell as a vertex and its four neighbours as edges, checking bounds. Track distance by processing the queue one level at a time or storing distances in an array. Use multi-source BFS by enqueueing all sources first, as in rotting oranges. BFS does not give shortest paths on weighted graphs; use Dijkstra there.

skills.name: Depth-first search
skills.notes: Depth-first search explores as far as possible along one path before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack, plus a visited set to avoid revisiting nodes and looping forever on cycles. With an adjacency list it runs in O(V + E) time and uses O(V) space, including the recursion stack, which can overflow on very deep graphs. DFS suits connected components, cycle detection, path existence, flood fill on grids, counting islands and topological sorting. In a directed graph a cycle exists when DFS meets a node that is still on the current recursion path, so track three states: unvisited, in progress and done. In an undirected graph a visited neighbour that is not the parent signals a cycle. DFS does not guarantee shortest paths. Be ready to write both recursive and iterative versions.

skills.name: Topological sort
skills.notes: A topological ordering of a directed acyclic graph lists vertices so that every edge goes from an earlier vertex to a later one. It exists only if the graph has no cycles, and detecting that no ordering exists is itself a typical question, as in course scheduling. Kahn's algorithm computes in-degrees, starts a queue with all zero in-degree vertices, repeatedly removes one, appends it to the order and decrements its neighbours' in-degrees, queueing those that reach zero. If the final order has fewer than V vertices the graph has a cycle. The DFS version adds a vertex to a list after all its descendants finish and reverses the list. Both run in O(V + E). The order is usually not unique. This is exactly the structure of skill prerequisites and build dependencies, where you must learn prerequisites first.

skills.name: Union-Find (disjoint sets)
skills.notes: Union-Find maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets with two operations: find returns the representative of an element's set and union merges two sets. Each set is a tree stored in a parent array. Without optimisation the tree can become a long chain and find costs O(n). Path compression flattens the tree during find, and union by rank or size attaches the smaller tree under the larger one; together they give nearly constant amortised time per operation, the inverse Ackermann function. Always union the roots, not the original elements. Typical uses are counting connected components, detecting cycles in an undirected graph, Kruskal's minimum spanning tree and grouping accounts or equivalent items. Two elements are connected exactly when their finds return the same root. Union-Find handles edge additions well but not edge deletions.

skills.name: Shortest paths and Dijkstra
skills.notes: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from one source to all vertices in a graph with non-negative edge weights. Keep a distance array initialised to infinity except zero for the source, and a min-heap of vertex and distance pairs. Repeatedly pop the closest unfinalised vertex and relax its outgoing edges: if dist[u] + w is smaller than dist[v], update dist[v] and push it. With a binary heap and adjacency lists the time is O((V + E) log V). Skip stale heap entries whose distance is larger than the recorded one. Dijkstra fails with negative edges because a finalised vertex could later be improved; use Bellman-Ford, which runs in O(VE) and detects negative cycles. On unweighted graphs plain BFS is enough and faster. Floyd-Warshall solves all pairs in O(V^3).

skills.name: Minimum spanning trees
skills.notes: A spanning tree of a connected undirected graph with V vertices uses exactly V minus one edges, connects every vertex and has no cycle; a minimum spanning tree has the smallest possible total weight. Kruskal's algorithm sorts all edges by weight and adds each edge if it connects two different components, checked with Union-Find, in O(E log E). Prim's algorithm grows a tree from one vertex, repeatedly adding the cheapest edge leaving the tree using a min-heap, in O((V + E) log V). Both rely on the cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST. If edge weights are distinct the MST is unique. An MST minimises total weight, not the path between two given vertices, so it is not the same as a shortest-path tree. A disconnected graph has a minimum spanning forest instead.

skills.name: Dynamic programming fundamentals
skills.notes: Dynamic programming solves problems whose solution can be built from solutions to overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure. Naive recursion repeats the same subproblems exponentially often; memoization caches each result the first time, and tabulation fills a table bottom up in dependency order. Either way the time becomes the number of distinct states times the work per state. The method is to define the state precisely, write the recurrence relating a state to smaller states, set base cases, and choose the iteration order. Fibonacci reduces from O(2^n) to O(n). Often a table can be compressed, for example keeping only the last two values for O(1) space. Dynamic programming differs from divide and conquer because subproblems overlap, and from greedy because it considers all choices of the recurrence rather than committing to one. Check by testing small cases by hand.

skills.name: One-dimensional DP
skills.notes: One-dimensional dynamic programming uses a single array where dp[i] depends on earlier entries. Classic problems include climbing stairs, where dp[i] equals dp[i-1] plus dp[i-2]; house robber, where dp[i] is the larger of skipping house i or taking it plus dp[i-2]; coin change for the minimum number of coins, where dp[a] equals one plus the minimum of dp[a - coin] over all coins; and longest increasing subsequence in O(n^2) or O(n log n) with binary search. State the meaning of dp[i] in one precise sentence, for example the best value using the first i items, then derive the recurrence. Initialise unreachable states with infinity and check for them before adding one. Often only the last few values are needed, reducing space to O(1). Compare with greedy to see when a greedy choice fails, such as coin change with unusual denominations.

skills.name: Two-dimensional DP
skills.notes: Two-dimensional dynamic programming has states described by two indices, such as positions in two strings or an item index and a capacity. For longest common subsequence, dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of one string and the first j of the other: if the characters match it is dp[i-1][j-1] plus one, otherwise the maximum of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1]. Edit distance is similar with three options: insert, delete and replace. The 0/1 knapsack has dp[i][w] as the best value using the first i items with capacity w, choosing to skip or take item i; its time is O(nW), which is pseudo-polynomial. Grid path counting uses dp[r][c] equals the sum from above and left. Fill the table in an order that respects dependencies, and compress to one row when only the previous row is needed. Subsequences need not be contiguous, unlike substrings.

skills.name: Greedy algorithms
skills.notes: A greedy algorithm builds a solution by repeatedly taking the locally best choice and never reconsidering it. It works only when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure, which you must justify with an exchange argument: show that any optimal solution can be transformed to include the greedy choice without getting worse. Classic correct examples are activity selection by earliest finish time, fractional knapsack by value per weight, Huffman coding, and jump game reachability. Classic failures include 0/1 knapsack and coin change with arbitrary denominations, where taking the largest coin first can miss the optimum, and these need dynamic programming. Sorting usually comes first, so many greedy solutions cost O(n log n). When unsure, test the greedy rule against small counterexamples or compare with brute force before trusting it.

skills.name: Interval problems

resources.title: Cracking the Coding Interview sorting and searching

skills.notes: Interval problems represent ranges as start and end pairs and usually start by sorting by start time. To merge overlapping intervals, sort, then keep a current interval and extend its end to the maximum when the next start is at most the current end; otherwise emit it and start a new one. Two intervals overlap when each starts before the other ends, and you must decide whether touching endpoints count as overlap. To insert a new interval into a sorted list, copy intervals ending before it, merge those overlapping it, then copy the rest. Minimum meeting rooms is the maximum number of simultaneous intervals, found with sorted start and end arrays or a min-heap of end times. Removing the fewest intervals to eliminate overlap is the greedy activity selection by earliest end. Sorting dominates, so these run in O(n log n).
